claims.text: A Cu-rich graded interlayer transitioning to an HEA composition will enhance adhesion of an HEA coating to a Cu matrix.
The graded interlayer will preserve the superior wear resistance of the HEA coating.
A Cu substrate is prone to adhesion problems with typical HEA coatings.
Thermal-expansion differences between Cu and typical HEA coatings contribute to adhesion problems.
Chemical-reactivity differences between Cu and typical HEA coatings contribute to adhesion problems.
A Cu-rich region or thin transition film can be deposited before the main HEA coating to create a graded interface.
Robust metallurgical bonding is critical under mechanical wear, friction, and moderate temperature fluctuations.
The proposed layer provides a gradual compositional and microstructural transition between the Cu substrate and HEA coating.
The graded interlayer minimizes thermal-expansion mismatch between the Cu substrate and refractory HEA.
The graded interlayer controls interfacial reactions between the Cu substrate and refractory HEA.
The tailored transition enhances metallurgical bonding.
Enhanced metallurgical bonding reduces coating debonding during wear.
HEAs possess high hardness and wear resistance.
A graded interlayer will improve HEA-coating adhesion relative to direct deposition on Cu.
A graded interlayer will maintain or enhance wear performance relative to direct deposition on Cu.
A directly deposited HEA coating on Cu is likely to have poor adhesion.
Thermal-expansion mismatch and deleterious interfacial reactions cause the anticipated poor adhesion of directly deposited HEA coatings on Cu.
The interlayer's effectiveness depends on precise control of its compositional gradient and processing parameters.
Extreme thermal cycling or an improperly engineered interlayer may prevent full mitigation of adhesion problems.
Surface and interface engineering trends support the use of graded interlayers to improve adhesion.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome allows wear resistance merely to be maintained, whereas the falsification rule treats any wear rate that is not improved as falsifying. Equal wear performance would therefore both satisfy the prediction and trigger falsification.
